name: Naga Heritage Village, Kisama
description: Permanent open-air complex 12 km south of Kohima between Kigwema and Phesama villages, holding morungs (bachelor dormitories) of all 17 recognised Naga tribes built in their distinct timber-and-thatch styles. Outside the 1-10 December Hornbill window the site is near-empty and the morungs become a quiet anthropology walk-through, with each Angami, Ao, Konyak and Sumi house keyed by carved horns over the entry posts.
why_hidden: Almost everyone visits during Hornbill week and treats it as a festival venue rather than a year-round museum-village; off-season Kisama gets a few dozen visitors a day.
best_time: January-March or July-September for solitude; 1-10 December for full Hornbill activation
how_to_reach: 12 km south of Kohima on NH-2 towards Imphal, 25 min by shared taxi from BOC junction, signed turnoff at Kisama gate
tips: Carry the Rs 30 entry slip from the gate office and ask the caretaker to unlock the WWII Museum on the same campus — it stays shut without a request

name: Ungma Village
description: Three kilometres south of Mokokchung town, Ungma is the oldest Ao Naga village and the dispersal point from which six Ao clans say they migrated after leaving their ancestral home at Chungliyimti. Wooden Tsongki morungs still stand at the village gates with the distinctive Ao log-drum (sungkong) houses on either side, and elders run an informal oral-history corner near the central church.
why_hidden: The 700-year lineage and active morungs are documented mostly on Mokokchung district government pages; tour itineraries skip Ungma in favour of Longkhum further out.
best_time: April-May around Moatsu festival (1-3 May) when traditional dress and granary rites are public
how_to_reach: 3 km south of Mokokchung town on the Mariani road, 10 min shared taxi or 35 min walk from main bazaar
tips: Ask at the village council office (Putu Menden) before photographing morungs — some are still in active ritual use

name: Mopungchuket Village
description: Government-declared rural tourism village (2007) on a ridge 15 km from Mokokchung, with stone-paved alleys, a small museum holding Ao headhunting-era daos and granary baskets, and a folklore park retelling the Jina-Etiben love legend through carved wooden tableaux. Often cited as the cleanest village in Nagaland — no plastic, fines for littering, garden patches outside every household.
why_hidden: Mokokchung itineraries default to Longkhum's viewpoint; Mopungchuket needs a 30-minute detour off the main road and most drivers will not propose it.
best_time: October-March for clear weather; avoid June-August monsoon when the unsealed approach turns slippery
how_to_reach: 15 km south-west of Mokokchung via Khensa-Longjang road, 45 min by hired vehicle (no shared taxi)
tips: Tea-stop at the lakeside pavilion below the museum — the caretaker will unlock the folklore park if you ask at the council office

name: Longkhum Village
description: One of the highest Ao villages at roughly 1,846 m, 17 km west of Mokokchung. The clouds settle below the ridgeline most mornings — locals call it the village of clouds — and the Lungkitsubu rock at the northern edge gives a 270-degree sweep across the Tsurang valley to Assam on clear days. The village still maintains a working morung used for the December Tsungrem Mong rites.
why_hidden: Day-trippers from Mokokchung peak in October but the village is bypassed in monsoon when fog rolls in and locals assume nobody will come.
best_time: October-February for clear distance views; April for cherry blossom along the approach road
how_to_reach: 17 km west of Mokokchung on the Longkhum road, 45 min by hired Sumo (shared service runs morning only)
tips: Walk the 1 km path from the village to Lungkitsubu rock at sunrise — by 9am tour vehicles arrive and the silence breaks

name: Longwa Village
description: Konyak village 42 km from Mon town where the Indo-Myanmar border runs through the Angh's house — by tradition the chief eats in India and sleeps in Myanmar. The hereditary Angh Tonyei Phawang is the 10th-generation ruler, and elders still wear the brass-skull headhunting necklaces and facial tattoos earned in the 1950s-60s raids. The village gunsmith works in a tin-roofed forge on the downward slope below the Angh's compound, hand-finishing muzzleloaders that local hunters still use.
why_hidden: Reaching Mon takes 11-12 hours of bad road from Dimapur and Longwa is another 3 hours beyond, so even Nagaland circuit travellers stop at Hornbill and turn back.
best_time: Aoleang festival 1-6 April for full ceremonial regalia; October-March for travel comfort
how_to_reach: 42 km north of Mon town on the Tizit-Longwa road, 3 hours by hired Sumo through Hongphoi and Chui villages
tips: Stay overnight at the Angh's guesthouse rather than day-tripping — the morning tea ritual at the chief's hearth is when the headhunting elders show up

name: Shangnyu Village
description: One of the oldest Konyak villages, 23 km from Mon, ruled by an Angh whose lineage holds a wooden fertility sculpture roughly 8 ft tall — carved naked figures, hornbills and a tiger — kept in a small village museum near the chief's house. The village was declared an ethnic-village reserve and academic anthropologists from JNU and Goettingen have catalogued the carvings since the 1960s.
why_hidden: The big Konyak headline is Longwa's border-house; Shangnyu needs its own day and gets dropped from condensed Mon itineraries.
best_time: October-April for stable roads; avoid May-September monsoon
how_to_reach: 23 km east of Mon town on the Aboi road, 1.5 hours by hired vehicle on rough metalled track
tips: Ask the Angh's family for the museum key — it isn't posted on the door, and you'll otherwise see only the locked exterior

name: Veda Peak
description: Highest peak in Mon district at roughly 1,950 m, a 3-4 hour pre-dawn drive from Mon town through Konyak hamlets. On clear winter mornings the silver thread of the Brahmaputra is visible across the Assam plains and the Patkai range fades into Myanmar to the east. The summit clearing has a small stone cairn and a single watchtower built by the Forest Department.
why_hidden: Mon visitors prioritise Longwa for the border-house and skip Veda; the road is unsealed and 4WD-only after October rain.
best_time: November-February for the Brahmaputra view; sunrise window 5.30-7am
how_to_reach: Roughly 50 km from Mon town via Aboi-Chen road then unsealed forest track, 4 hours one-way by 4WD only
tips: Leave Mon by 2.30am to catch sunrise; carry a fleece — temperatures drop below 5C even in March

name: Semoma Fort
description: Hilltop ruin at the eastern edge of Khonoma village where Angami warriors fought their final stand against the British in November 1879 after the Battle of Khonoma broke the back of Naga resistance. A stone inscription erected by the village council names the fallen and Major John Butler's contemporary report calling it 'one of the strongest forts in North East India' is reproduced on a brass plaque nearby. Walls are largely gone but the terraced fortifications and gate posts remain.
why_hidden: The eco-tourism narrative around Khonoma's green-village status drowns out the warrior-history layer; most homestay guests don't get walked here.
best_time: October-March for clear weather and dry trail
how_to_reach: 20-min uphill walk from Khonoma village square via the eastern church path; ask at the village tourism desk for a guide
tips: Pair with the Angami martyrs' tombstones at the village entry — the fort makes more sense after reading the names

name: Khonoma Nature & Tragopan Sanctuary
description: Twenty square kilometres of community-protected forest declared by Khonoma's village council in 1998 after 300 Blyth's tragopans were killed in a single hunting competition the year before. India's only village-managed sanctuary for the endangered Blyth's tragopan, with 196 documented bird species including hill partridge and dark-rumped swift. Trails are maintained by the Khonoma Youth Organisation and a local guide is mandatory.
why_hidden: Birding circuits go to Eaglenest in Arunachal; Khonoma's sanctuary requires booking through the village council a day ahead, which most tour operators don't bother with.
best_time: March-May for tragopan breeding-season calls and rhododendron bloom; pre-dawn slot
how_to_reach: Trailhead at western edge of Khonoma village, 8 km loop or 14 km traverse to Dzulekie; permit and guide from Khonoma Tourism Development Board
tips: Tragopan sightings need a 4.30am start and silence on the trail — the bird is hyper-shy and bolts at voices

name: Dzulekie Village
description: Tiny Angami hamlet 8 km west of Khonoma at the bottom of a forested gorge, with a clear stream running past stone-stacked terrace fields and a single trout-rearing pond run by the village fisheries cooperative. Cooler than Khonoma by 3-4C in summer and used by Khonoma residents themselves as a weekend escape. A short trail from the village leads to a 30 m waterfall locals call Dzulekie falls.
why_hidden: Most Khonoma visitors do a day-trip from Kohima and turn back without ever descending to Dzulekie; the road continues past the green-village showpiece into territory most itineraries don't list.
best_time: April-June for trout and waterfall flow; October for clear ridge-views above the village
how_to_reach: 8 km west of Khonoma village via the sanctuary road, 25 min by hired vehicle or 2-hour walk through the Tragopan trail
tips: Ring ahead through Khonoma's tourism desk to arrange lunch at the cooperative — there are no commercial eateries

name: Japfu Peak Ridge
description: At 3,014 m the highest peak in Kohima district, sharing the same range as Dzukou and reachable as a side-traverse from the Dzukou rest house by experienced trekkers. The summit ridge holds the 109-foot rhododendron tree certified in the Guinness Book as the world's tallest, blooming crimson in March-April. From the top, Saramati and the Patkai roll east into Myanmar and Kohima town is a grid of corrugated roofs to the north.
why_hidden: Most Dzukou trekkers stop at the valley floor and turn back; the Japfu add-on adds a hard 6-hour day and is rarely sold as a package.
best_time: March-April for rhododendron bloom; November for clearest distance views
how_to_reach: Day-traverse from Dzukou rest house via the south ridge, 6 hours up-and-back; guide mandatory, arrange via Viswema village council
tips: Camp at the rest house the night before and start by 4am to clear the summit before mid-morning cloud roll-in

name: Viswema Village Morung
description: Southern Angami village at the Dzukou trailhead, with a working morung at the village centre where the Viswema Youth Society runs the trek-permit desk and trains young porters. Stone-paved village lanes climb past terraced rice fields to a viewpoint over the Lanyu valley. The village is the staging point for the Viswema route, easier than Jakhama, and most trekkers pass through without stopping.
why_hidden: Trekkers treat Viswema as a parking lot and head straight up; the village itself sees almost zero overnight visitors despite running the trek economy.
best_time: October-April for trekking season; May-July if combining with Dzukou Lily bloom
how_to_reach: 25 km south of Kohima on NH-2, 45 min by shared taxi from BOC junction; trek permit office at Viswema community hall
tips: Pick up the Rs 100 trek permit and porter contacts here rather than at the trailhead — the rate doubles further up

name: Dzukou Rest House Stream
description: Spring-fed stream running 200 m below the Dzukou rest house through a fold in the bamboo grass, used by trekkers as the only water source on the valley floor. Late June through August the banks are pink with the endemic Dzukou Lily (Lilium chitrangadae) — found nowhere else on earth — and you can hear the water from the rest-house porch. The valley sits in the crater of an extinct volcano so the stream traces the old caldera floor.
why_hidden: Day-hikers go to the cross at the valley overlook and turn back without descending to the stream; the lily section needs a further 30-min walk most groups skip.
best_time: Late June to mid-August for Dzukou Lily bloom; September for clear water and remaining wildflowers
how_to_reach: 200 m descent from Dzukou rest house on the marked southern path; total 13 km from Viswema trailhead
tips: Don't pluck the lilies — fines from the village forest committee are Rs 5,000 and locals do check

name: Glory Peak
description: Roughly 2,600 m peak 3-4 km from Pfutsero town, reached by a stone-paved trail through pine forest that turns to alpine grass near the top. On crystal mornings between November and February — about 15 days a year — Mount Everest is visible to the north-west and Saramati (Nagaland's highest) sits clean to the east. The Phek district tourism department maintains a single bamboo treehouse at the summit clearing.
why_hidden: Pfutsero itself is a 6-7 hour drive from Kohima and rarely on Nagaland circuits; the Everest-visibility window is so narrow most visitors miss it.
best_time: November-February for distance views and frost on the trail; sunrise window 5.30-6.30am
how_to_reach: 4 km hike from Pfutsero town via the Glory Peak trail; trailhead signed at the BSNL tower junction
tips: Stay overnight in Pfutsero and walk up before dawn — by 9am cloud cover almost always closes the Everest line

name: Kapamodzu Peak
description: Tabletop mountain at 2,620 m above Zhavame village, listed by Nagaland Tourism as the highest tabletop in the state. The summit plateau is a flat alpine grass platform around half a kilometre across, with views into Manipur to the south and the Saramati-Japfu line to the north. Pre-trek night is spent at the Zhavame village morung and the climb runs 4 hours each way.
why_hidden: Featured on the state tourism site but with almost no commercial trekking infrastructure; you have to arrange village hosts directly.
best_time: October-March for clear views and dry trail; avoid June-September monsoon
how_to_reach: Trailhead at Zhavame village, 35 km from Pfutsero on the Phek-Chizami road; 1.5 hours by hired vehicle to Zhavame, then 4-hour climb
tips: Arrange the trek through Zhavame village council a day ahead — there is no signage and no GPS-tagged trail

name: Chizami Weaves Workshop
description: Chakhesang women's weaving collective in Chizami village, 25 km from Pfutsero, that has built a sustainable-livelihood model around traditional loin-loom textiles since 2008. The workshop floor holds 30+ active backstrap looms and visitors can sit in on natural-dye sessions using stick-lac, indigo and walnut bark. The collective supplies designers in Delhi and Mumbai and runs a small retail counter selling shawls, mekhalas and table runners directly.
why_hidden: Chizami sits 25 km off the Pfutsero road and the workshop isn't on regular itineraries — most visitors only learn of it through the North East Network referral chain.
best_time: October-March; weekdays only (the weavers don't run sessions on Sundays)
how_to_reach: 25 km north-east of Pfutsero on the Phek-Chizami road, 1 hour by hired vehicle; workshop signed at Chizami village council
tips: Email or call North East Network's Chizami office a day ahead to confirm a weaver is in — drop-ins find the doors open but no demonstration
